item.title: Improving Developer Experience in the Age of Agents
item.description: Coding agents may be changing how developers work - what does that mean for developer experience? Here's how we are starting to think about both.
item.content:encoded:
When agents write the code, what is left for developers to do? We don't know for sure, but most would agree that there's no going back. Times, indeed, they are a-change-in.

And for a smaller group of us building developer tools - there's another question: what does it mean for developer experience (DX)?

We take care to craft API surfaces, documentation and learning material to guide developers to the right syntax, and help them discover the right tools.

Does any of it still matter when an agent is the one reading it? It's easy to imagine that none of it would make a difference to our omniscient future overlords.

But here are two things that I think. One, we shouldn't forget that (at least for now) there is a human at the end of the agent, pulling the strings. So we should look to optimise their experience. And two, the principles behind good DX still apply, even when agents encounter problems that human readers never see.

Let me tell you about a recent effort to improve our documentation. I found that in some cases, agents were drawing incorrect conclusions from our documentation. When we dug in, we traced the root cause to the fact that some agents were not receiving complete documentation pages! Pages were truncated, code examples were missing for some languages, and sections were missing.

And that missing context, we found, would send an agent searching elsewhere or lead it to draw incorrect conclusions or write wrong code. These issues had gone unnoticed because they affected a class of readers that rarely tells us when something is wrong: coding agents. And as a kicker - some of those issues would only exist for agents!

The same page can look different to every agent​

So how did we find out what agents were actually seeing?

When it comes to identifying DX issues, we might have turned to user interviews. For agents, we focused on observing their behaviour directly.

We set up several agents to run the same task in a repeatable way, and explored their logs and outputs. This let us see not only the final answers, but the paths they took to get there: what tools they used, what searches they ran, and what pages they read.

Sure, this identified documentation pages to update. But importantly, it showed us that agents should be treated as a different class of reader.

For one, agents do not read web pages in the same way as people using a browser. Fetch tools in different coding environments can return different parts of a page, and often do not tell the site when content is missing.

But here's the important part: even if an agent notices missing information, it is unlikely to report the problem to us as the documentation maintainers. It may simply search elsewhere or work around it.

Once we could reproduce those failures, we could test potential fixes: change the documentation, run the same tasks again, and check whether agents received the context they needed.

For example, before our changes, one fetch tool returned the correct language examples in only 7 of 15 TypeScript runs and 3 of 15 Go runs. After the changes, it returned the right snippets in every run we checked.

We also found an outdated sentence on a concepts page that led agents to use an older client library, even though that page was not where the code examples lived. After we corrected it, every answer we checked used the current client.

When useful content is missing, agents may try to work around it by finding raw source files or downloading a page and writing a parser. In one example, an agent took 23 turns to reach a solution when the needed code was hidden; with the Markdown version of the page, it took 6. We also shipped Markdown versions of our documentation pages, reducing token use on page loads by around 20%.

These tests helped us catch regressions, too. A change that fixed hidden code tabs caused one fetch tool to return a section of the Quickstart while dropping the rest. Re-running the tests exposed the problem, and a small layout change fixed it.

DX and agent experience work together​

These are examples of agent experience (AX): making sure agents can use our docs, tools, and APIs effectively. As more work is delegated to agents, their experience matters alongside the experience of developers using those same resources directly.

The goal of DX has never been simply to make writing code faster. It is to reduce friction between a developer and the value they are trying to create. Code is one part of that. Developers still need to understand the problem, give agents good instructions, set up the right environment, and verify the result.

That means a good experience needs to serve both the developer and the agent working between the developer and the product:

For developers, that means helping them make sound architectural decisions, communicate their intent to agents, and verify outcomes. For agents, it means making information complete and discoverable, providing agent-appropriate tools, reducing ambiguity, and making correctness observable.

Those goals align with Don Norman's ideas of the "gulf of execution" and "gulf of evaluation": people need to understand how to act and whether their actions worked. Agents change the interfaces and mechanisms involved, but those underlying needs remain.

Turning the principles into practice​

We are applying these ideas to the tools and workflows developers use with Weaviate. For example, when asked to update a Go service that uses the v5 client after GraphQL is disabled, some agents tried to call the server's gRPC API directly instead of looking for the newer Go v6 client. We are exploring ways to guide them toward the supported client with as little extra effort from the developer as possible.

We are also measuring how well agents can build Weaviate applications from scratch and adapt them to a developer's needs. That includes using current capabilities such as the HFresh index, Rotational Quantization, and PathSeer filtering, as well as applying the best practices we have learned.

Other work includes exploring what an agent-oriented Quickstart could look like, and how agents could help with cluster maintenance and troubleshooting.

The principle stays the same​

The core practice is familiar: find where people get stuck, improve the experience, and verify that the improvement worked. What has changed is the set of users and tools we need to measure. Developers now work through coding agents as well as IDEs and browsers, and agents rarely tell us when they could not find or understand something.

That makes measurement more important, not less. By testing how agents use our docs and tools before and after changes, we can reduce friction for both the developer and the agent—and help developers get more value from their work.

Ready to start building?​

Check out the Quickstart tutorial, or sign up for a free Weaviate Cloud account.

item.title: Weaviate 1.40 Release
item.description: Weaviate 1.40 makes dropping a named vector and 4-bit Rotational Quantization GA, adds multi-vector embeddings on HFresh and PathSeer filtering, and changes vector configuration defaults.
item.content:encoded:
Weaviate v1.40 is now available open-source and on Weaviate Cloud.

Two features reach general availability in this release: dropping a named vector, which frees the disk and index memory an unused vector was holding, and 4-bit Rotational Quantization. Two more are new: the HFresh index now takes multi-vector embeddings through MUVERA, and PathSeer joins ACORN and sweeping as a third filter strategy for HNSW. This post also catches up on the Search REST API, which changed a lot over the 1.39 patch line. It also covers a breaking change to vector configuration defaults to check before you upgrade.

Here are the release highlights!

  • Drop a named vector - General Availability
  • 4-bit Rotational Quantization - General Availability
  • Multi-vector embeddings on HFresh with MUVERA
  • PathSeer filter strategy
  • Search REST API (Preview)
  • Vector configuration defaults (breaking change)
  • Performance Improvements and Fixes
  • Community Contributions
  • Summary
Breaking change

If your server sets DEFAULT_VECTORIZER_MODULE, read Vector configuration defaults before you upgrade.

Drop a named vector - General Availability​

Collections pick up vectors over time. You add a named vector to try a new embedding model, the new one wins, and the old one stays on every object, in every shard, taking up disk and index memory. Until now the only way out was to re-create the collection and re-import everything.

v1.40 makes the drop vector index endpoint generally available. It has existed since v1.37 as an experimental feature that was off by default. In v1.40 it is on by default.

A drop deletes the vector's index and removes its embedding from every object. The collection's other named vectors and all object data stay as they are.

A drop cannot be undone

To get the vector back, add it again and then re-vectorize or re-import your objects.

How it works​

With the Python client (4.24.0 or newer), call delete_vector_index with the name of the vector:

articles = client.collections.use("Article")
articles.config.delete_vector_index("body_vector")

Over REST it is one DELETE request:

curl -X DELETE \
  http://localhost:8080/v1/schema/Article/vectors/body_vector/index

The call returns once Weaviate has accepted the drop. The cleanup itself runs in the background, shard by shard, and picks up where it left off after a restart.

While the cleanup runs, the vector is still listed in the collection definition, and writes that target it are rejected. In a batch, only the objects that carry the dropped vector fail. The drop is finished when the vector disappears from the definition.

A few more things to know:

  • Permissions: You need update permission on the collection and on its data objects, because a drop rewrites every object.
  • Inactive tenants: A tenant that is inactive holds up completion until it is activated and a later cleanup round reaches it.
  • Reusing the name: Once the drop is finished you can add a vector with the same name again, even with a different dimensionality. The new index starts empty.
  • The last vector: Dropping the only vector leaves a collection with no vectors. Objects and properties stay.

The Python client is the first to wrap the endpoint. From any other language, send the REST request.

Related resources
  • How-to: Manage collections - Drop a named vector
  • References: RESTful API - Schema

4-bit Rotational Quantization - General Availability​

4-bit Rotational Quantization (RQ), a preview in v1.39, is now generally available. RQ rotates each vector, then stores every dimension as a small integer instead of a full float.

The reason to turn it on is memory. On a million 1536-dimension vectors, 4-bit RQ used about 45% less memory than 8-bit RQ. A cluster of the same size holds more vectors, or you run a smaller one. Imports get faster too.

Search quality holds up because Weaviate rescores the best candidates with the original vectors.

How it works​

Many embedding models produce vectors that cluster around a point that is not zero. Centering, in Weaviate since v1.39.3, measures that point from a sample of your data and compresses relative to it. That brings 4-bit recall close to 8-bit. It is off by default because some models already do this. It only applies to 4-bit.

Set rq.bits = 4 on an HNSW index. With Python client 4.23.1 or newer, turn on centering in the same call:

from weaviate.classes.config import Configure

client.collections.create(
    "Doc",
    vector_config=Configure.Vectors.self_provided(
        name="default",
        vector_index_config=Configure.VectorIndex.hnsw(
            quantizer=Configure.VectorIndex.Quantizer.rq(bits=4, centering=True),
        ),
    ),
)

bits locks when RQ is first enabled on a vector, so pick the width before then. You can still enable RQ later on an uncompressed collection.

Operators can set DEFAULT_QUANTIZATION=rq-4 to make 4-bit RQ the default for new HNSW indexes. Weaviate Cloud keeps 8-bit RQ as its default. 4-bit works on HNSW indexes only.

The numbers and the engineering are in the 4-bit Rotational Quantization deep dive.

Related resources
  • Concepts: Vector quantization - Rotational quantization
  • How-to: Compression - 4-bit RQ
  • Blog: 4-bit Rotational Quantization

Multi-vector embeddings on HFresh with MUVERA​

HFresh is Weaviate's disk-based vector index. It keeps a small index of centroids in memory and stores compressed vectors on disk, so it needs far less memory than HNSW. Until now it only took one vector per object.

Late-interaction models such as ColBERT and ColPali produce a multi-vector embedding: one vector per token or image patch, instead of one vector per object. They rank well, but a page of text can turn into hundreds of vectors, which is the kind of data that strains memory. In v1.40, HFresh can index them.

There is one condition. On HFresh, multi-vector embeddings need MUVERA encoding. MUVERA turns a set of vectors into a single fixed-length vector, so HFresh can search it like any other.

How it works​

A multi-vector query on HFresh runs in three passes:

searchProbe and rq.rescoreLimit, both set in the HFresh index config, control the first two passes. searchProbe sets how many posting lists are scanned. rq.rescoreLimit sets how many candidates survive the rescore. The survivors are then scored exactly against their original token vectors with MaxSim. MaxSim is the late-interaction score that matches each query token to its closest document token.

To set it up, create a named vector with no vectorizer, MUVERA encoding, and an HFresh index:

from weaviate.classes.config import Configure

client.collections.create(
    "Page",
    vector_config=Configure.MultiVectors.self_provided(
        name="colbert",
        encoding=Configure.VectorIndex.MultiVector.Encoding.muvera(),
        vector_index_config=Configure.VectorIndex.hfresh(),
    ),
)

The constraints:

  • The vector needs "vectorizer": "none": You bring the token vectors yourself.
  • MUVERA is required, and fixed at creation: multivector.muvera.enabled cannot be changed later.
  • The encoding is always compressed with 1-bit RQ: PQ, SQ and BQ are rejected, and RQ cannot be turned off.
multivector.enabled alone is not enough on HFresh

If you set multivector.enabled without MUVERA, the collection is created, but it behaves as a regular vector without multi-vector support and rejects multi-vector imports and queries. Set multivector.muvera.enabled.

Related resources
  • Config references: Multi-vector embeddings on HFresh
  • Concepts: Multi-vector embeddings on HFresh
  • How-to: Multi-vector compression - MUVERA encoding
  • Blog: HFresh, memory-efficient vector search

PathSeer filter strategy​

A filtered vector search has to find the nearest objects that also pass a filter. On an HNSW index, the filterStrategy setting decides how the search walks the graph when many neighbors fail the filter. Until now you had two choices: acorn (the default) and sweeping.

v1.40 adds a third, pathseer. It comes from the SIGMOD 2026 paper by Zhiyue Li et al., and the paper's first author, @lizhiyuell, contributed the implementation (#12137).

In Weaviate's benchmarks PathSeer was the fastest strategy, or within a few percent of it, on random, topical and combined filters. ACORN stays ahead only on strongly negatively correlated filters, where the filter all but excludes the query's neighborhood. The PathSeer post has the full benchmarks and a walkthrough of the algorithm.

How it works​

PathSeer walks the bottom layer of the graph like sweeping. While the result set is still filling, it also filter-checks the neighbors of each candidate's neighbors, like ACORN. Once the result set is full, it skips the non-matching neighbors of a non-matching candidate without computing their distance. It makes that call per node, so there is no new parameter to tune.

It stores nothing extra. There is no import cost, no memory overhead, and you can switch an existing collection to it, or away from it, without reindexing. The flat-search cutoff still applies first: when a filter matches fewer objects than flatSearchCutoff, Weaviate scans those objects instead of walking the graph.

To switch an existing named vector over:

from weaviate.classes.config import Reconfigure, VectorFilterStrategy

articles = client.collections.use("Article")
articles.config.update(
    vector_config=Reconfigure.Vectors.update(
        name="default",
        vector_index_config=Reconfigure.VectorIndex.hnsw(
            filter_strategy=VectorFilterStrategy.PATHSEER,
        ),
    )
)

In a collection definition sent over REST, it is one field in the HNSW vectorIndexConfig:

{ "vectorIndexConfig": { "filterStrategy": "pathseer" } }
Related resources
  • Concepts: Filtering - PathSeer
  • Blog: PathSeer, adaptive filtered vector search

Search REST API (Preview)​

The Search REST API lets you search with plain JSON over HTTP/1.1, with no generated client and no GraphQL query strings. It arrived as an experimental, off-by-default feature in v1.39. A lot has changed since then. All of it shipped in 1.39 patches, and the API is now a preview.

  • On by default from v1.39.7
  • Structured references from v1.39.3: A new returnReferences field replaces the dotted "hasAuthor.name" form the 1.39 post warned about. A dotted name in returnProperties is now rejected.
  • near-vector from v1.39.8: It takes a vector you supply, so it works on collections without a vectorizer.

That makes six endpoints:

  • POST /v1/search/{collection}/near-text
  • POST /v1/search/{collection}/bm25
  • POST /v1/search/{collection}/hybrid
  • POST /v1/search/{collection}/near-object
  • POST /v1/search/{collection}/near-vector
  • POST /v1/aggregate/{collection} (returns a count)

How it works​

Here is a near-vector search that also follows a reference to each book's author:

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/search/Book/near-vector \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"vector":[0.1,0.9,0.2],"limit":1,
       "returnProperties":["title"],
       "returnReferences":[{"linkOn":"writtenBy","returnProperties":["name"]}],
       "returnMetadata":["distance"]}'

Each returnReferences entry names the reference property in linkOn and what to return from the objects it points to. You can also set targetCollection for a multi-target reference, returnMetadata for the referenced objects, and a nested returnReferences to go one hop further. Referenced objects come back in the same properties and metadata shape as the top-level hits:

{
  "results": [
    {
      "id": "ce442a4d-a704-46bd-b5c3-cf7b1b2ffdc0",
      "metadata": { "distance": 0.00040352345 },
      "properties": { "title": "The Left Hand of Darkness" },
      "references": {
        "writtenBy": [{ "properties": { "name": "Ursula K. Le Guin" } }]
      }
    }
  ],
  "tookMs": 1
}

A few things have not changed. The default limit is QUERY_DEFAULTS_LIMIT (10). targetVector takes a single vector name. No client library wraps these endpoints yet. Boost, MMR, reranking, generative search and grouped search are not available over REST.

Preview

The Search REST API is a preview feature. Its request and response shape may still change in future releases.

Related resources
  • References: RESTful API - Search endpoints

Vector configuration defaults (breaking change)​

Check this before you upgrade

If your server sets DEFAULT_VECTORIZER_MODULE, collections you create on v1.40 without naming a vectorizer will not be vectorized. There is no error at creation time, only a warning at startup.

From v1.40, DEFAULT_VECTORIZER_MODULE is deprecated and ignored. Weaviate logs a warning at startup if it is set. The default top-level vectorizer is always none. Existing collections are not affected. What changes is what a new collection definition gives you:

Your collection definition setsBefore v1.40From v1.40
No vector parameters at allA single-vector collection, filled in from the server defaultsA collection without a vector
vectorIndexType or vectorIndexConfig, but no vectorizerA single-vector collection, vectorized by DEFAULT_VECTORIZER_MODULEA single-vector collection that does not vectorize
An explicit vectorizerUnchangedUnchanged

Older clients that always send vectorIndexType, such as the Python client before 4.21.2, land in the second row. Auto-schema changed earlier: since v1.39.1 it creates a named vector called default with the vectorizer set to none.

What to do: name the vectorizer explicitly in every collection definition that needs one, before you upgrade.

Related resources
  • Migration guide: Vector configuration defaults
  • Config references: Collections without a vector

Performance Improvements and Fixes​

Beyond the headline features, v1.40 ships a long list of improvements. Some of the items below first shipped in 1.39 patches, and those say so. A few worth calling out:

  • Shard status per replica: GET /v1/schema/{collection}/shards now reports a per_node_status object that maps each node to the shard's status on that node. A replica that cannot be reached, or cannot serve reads, reports UNAVAILABLE. The old status and vectorQueueSize fields are deprecated.
  • Stricter MCP hybrid tool: the built-in MCP server's hybrid search tool now rejects an alpha outside 0 to 1 and a negative limit. It combines results with relative score fusion, the same default as the other APIs, and it rejects unknown argument keys.
  • gRPC for Google Cloud Storage backups: the backup-gcs module now talks to GCS over gRPC by default. A local emulator that only serves the JSON API needs GCS_MODULE_TRANSPORT=http.
  • Smaller HNSW graph in memory: each HNSW node is now a single heap object instead of three, which means less memory per node and fewer allocations. Shipped in v1.39.6.
  • Leaner aggregations: aggregation scans now reuse their buffers and read each segment through a single reader, so they allocate much less. Shipped in v1.39.3.
  • A read_backups permission: a role can now list backups and read backup and restore status without being able to create, restore or cancel one. Shipped in v1.39.10.
  • Two new generative modules: DigitalOcean arrived in v1.39.2 and Meta AI in v1.39.3.
Related resources
  • Weaviate 1.40: GitHub Release Notes

Community Contributions​

Weaviate is open source, and this release cycle includes work from four first-time contributors. Thank you to:

  • @lizhiyuell: the PathSeer filter strategy for HNSW (#12137)
  • @hamodywe: fetching Boost.Depth-deep candidates in hybrid sub-searches (#12537) (since v1.39.1)
  • @bharadwaj-pendyala: excluding LSM scratch files from the offload-s3 shard upload (#12884)
  • @ColtonRobak: passing the tenant to the re-vectorize check on PATCH (#13345) (since v1.39.8)

If you'd like to contribute, check out the contributor guide and the good-first-issue label on GitHub.

Summary​

Weaviate v1.40 promotes two features to general availability, brings multi-vector embeddings to HFresh, and adds a third HNSW filter strategy.

Key highlights:

  • Drop a named vector (GA): remove a vector you no longer need from every object, in the background, without re-creating the collection
  • 4-bit Rotational Quantization (GA): close to half the memory of 8-bit RQ on HNSW indexes, with optional centering to keep recall high
  • Multi-vector embeddings on HFresh with MUVERA: ColBERT and ColPali style embeddings on the disk-based index, through MUVERA encoding
  • PathSeer filter strategy: a third way to walk the HNSW graph under a filter, from a SIGMOD 2026 paper, switchable on existing collections
  • Search REST API (Preview): on by default, structured references, and a near-vector endpoint, all since the 1.39 patch line
  • Vector configuration defaults (breaking change): DEFAULT_VECTORIZER_MODULE is ignored, so name your vectorizer in every collection definition before you upgrade

Ready to get started?

The release is available open-source on GitHub and on Weaviate Cloud, where you can spin up a cluster on the free tier.

note

Not all features may be available on Weaviate Cloud. Preview and experimental features, and anything that needs specific environment configuration, may not be enabled on managed clusters, or may arrive there on a different schedule.

If you are upgrading a self-hosted cluster, check the migration guide for version-specific notes.

Thanks for reading, and happy vector searching!

Ready to start building?​

Check out the Quickstart tutorial, or sign up for a free Weaviate Cloud account.

item.title: Deprecating the GraphQL API: timeline and migration paths
item.description: Weaviate's GraphQL API is deprecated as of October 26, 2026. See the timeline for Weaviate Cloud and self-hosted, who is affected, and how to migrate.
item.content:encoded:
GraphQL was Weaviate's first query API, and many of you have built on it since our earliest releases. Today we are deprecating it. Nothing breaks today. Clusters that use GraphQL keep it until May 1, 2027, the end-of-life date for GraphQL on Weaviate Cloud. We can help you through the migration. Contact our support team through the support portal or at support@weaviate.io, whatever your setup looks like. The GraphQL migration guide walks you through the move, and this post explains why, what happens when, and what your options are.

In short
  • The GraphQL API is deprecated as of October 26, 2026. Nothing breaks on that day.
  • Weaviate Cloud switches GraphQL off on all clusters on May 1, 2027. May 1, 2027 is the end-of-life date for GraphQL on Weaviate Cloud. If your cluster has not used GraphQL in the last 30 days, it is switched off on December 1, 2026. New Weaviate Cloud clusters are already created without GraphQL.
  • We are emailing all Weaviate Cloud customers so you know whether your clusters are affected.
  • If you are on Weaviate Cloud and need help, contact support through the support portal or at support@weaviate.io.
  • Every Weaviate version released before May 1, 2027 keeps a working GraphQL API. The first minor release after that date disables it by default, and you can switch it back on. It is removed in a later release.
  • If your application searches through a current Python, TypeScript, Java or C# client, you are most likely not affected. Everyone else should follow the migration guide.

Modernizing Weaviate's query API​

GraphQL served Weaviate and its users well for a long time. It gave you one readable language for every kind of search, and a lot of what you built on Weaviate went through it. We are proud of that work. We are moving to one modern query API, and here is what you gain:

  • Speed: gRPC sends binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, so queries use less bandwidth and return faster than JSON over HTTP. The gRPC performance post has the measurements.

  • Clear contracts: Typed messages give every client typed results and generated request objects, so there is no query string to assemble and no nested JSON to parse. Errors arrive as real status codes, not as HTTP 200 with an errors array. Metadata is a field on the result, not a separate _additional block.

  • Security that fits fine-grained access: GraphQL introspection needs read permission on every collection. That does not fit role-based access control (RBAC) with per-collection permissions. The gRPC and REST APIs check exactly the collection you query.

  • Built for how queries are written today: GraphQL's strength was a query language you could read and type by hand. Today most queries are built by client libraries, frameworks and agents. A compact binary protocol and a plain JSON API serve them better than a hand-written query language.

  • Scales to many collections: A Weaviate instance with many collections is a use case we see more and more often. However, if you have a large number of collections (e.g. 1000+), each addition or removal of a collection may take a significant amount of time as it requires a rebuild of the full GraphQL schema. Retiring GraphQL eliminates this bottleneck.

One API also means every search feature is built, tested and documented once, which lets us ship improvements faster.

Timeline​

Are you affected?​

This only affects you if you send queries to Weaviate over GraphQL. Here is how to tell whether you do.

Your own code sends GraphQL:

  • It sends HTTP requests to /v1/graphql directly.
  • It calls a raw GraphQL helper in a client, such as graphql_raw_query() in Python.
  • Browser code in your application posts GraphQL queries.

A client or tool sends it for you:

  • An older client: the Python v3 API (weaviate.Client), weaviate-ts-client v2, the Java client v5, or the Go client v5 and earlier send queries over GraphQL.
  • A no-code or BI tool that sends GraphQL to your cluster.

The guide explains how to find your GraphQL usage.

If you reach Weaviate through a framework such as LangChain or LlamaIndex, use the official Weaviate integration built on a current client. A community package may still send GraphQL.

What to use instead​

Client libraries (recommended)​

The current Python, TypeScript, Java and C# clients search over gRPC, and they are the path we recommend. If you use Go, the move is to the v6 client, which uses gRPC. See the client libraries section in the guide.

TypeScript web client​

For browsers and edge runtimes that cannot open a native gRPC connection, the TypeScript web client (@weaviate/web) uses gRPC-Web. It is available now, with the same API as the Node client. See the TypeScript client for web.

REST Search API​

For stacks that cannot run a client at all, the REST Search API offers plain JSON endpoints for search and aggregation (see the REST API reference). It is in Preview today. It is a subset of what GraphQL offers, so check the queries without a REST equivalent yet before you start.

A few GraphQL-only features have no equivalent today. The guide lists them under GraphQL features without an equivalent. We are committed to covering what our customers need. If anything you rely on is not covered, reach out to support and we will work on adding it.

How to migrate​

The migration guide maps GraphQL queries to their replacements. There are six months between the deprecation and the end of life on Weaviate Cloud, so you can plan the move around your own releases. And you can switch GraphQL off on your own instance today, so you find out if anything breaks.

  1. Find your GraphQL calls: Search your code, proxies and tools for /v1/graphql and raw GraphQL helpers. See find your GraphQL usage.
  2. Pick a path: Use a client library where you can, the TypeScript web client in the browser, and the REST Search API where neither fits. The guide has a decision table for this.
  3. Convert your queries: Use the Migration guide to map existing GraphQL queries to alternative methods.
  4. Verify with GraphQL disabled: Run your application against a Weaviate instance with GraphQL turned off. On Weaviate Cloud, contact support and we switch GraphQL off on a cluster of your choice so you can test. See test with GraphQL disabled.
One query, four ways

Here is one near-text search on a Movie collection, written four ways: five "space opera" movies from 1980 or later in the scifi category, with title, year and distance.

  • GraphQL (deprecated)
  • Python client
  • TypeScript web client
  • REST Search API
{
  Get {
    Movie(
      nearText: { concepts: ["space opera"] }
      limit: 5
      where: {
        operator: And
        operands: [
          { path: ["year"], operator: GreaterThanEqual, valueInt: 1980 }
          { path: ["category"], operator: Equal, valueText: "scifi" }
        ]
      }
    ) {
      title
      year
      _additional {
        distance
      }
    }
  }
}
from weaviate.classes.query import Filter, MetadataQuery

movies = client.collections.use("Movie")

response = movies.query.near_text(
    query="space opera",
    limit=5,
    filters=(
        Filter.by_property("year").greater_or_equal(1980)
        & Filter.by_property("category").equal("scifi")
    ),
    return_properties=["title", "year"],

item.title: Weaviate security release - Medium severity fix for a cross-collection vector disclosure in nearObject (CVE pending assignment)
item.description: Weaviate v1.39.3 fixes a medium-severity authorization issue in the nearObject GraphQL operator.
item.content:encoded:
Intro​

With the release of Weaviate v1.39.3 and >, there is a fix for a medium severity authorization vulnerability in Weaviate's GraphQL nearObject search operator, where a user could read the vector of an object in a collection they do not have permission to read. A CVE has been requested from MITRE and is pending assignment; we will update this post with the CVE ID once it has been issued.

As per our security policy, Weaviate customers running in Weaviate Cloud, and Marketplace customers on AWS, Azure and GCP have been patched seamlessly. Our Weaviate Enterprise Support customers have received early notification under embargo, and our customer-facing teams are working with Weaviate Dedicated customers to organize version upgrades where appropriate.

Cross-collection vector disclosure via nearObject (CVE pending assignment)​

A nearObject search takes a beacon naming an existing object, loads that object's vector, and uses it as the search vector. Weaviate authorized the collection being searched, but did not authorize the collection named in the beacon. Where the two differed, the vector of the beacon target was loaded and used even if the caller had no read permission on it.

The result is not a direct read of the protected object. The caller never sees the object, its properties or its vector in the response. What the caller does receive is the distance between the protected vector and each object returned by the search, and those distances are enough to reconstruct the protected vector. By populating a collection they do control with chosen probe vectors and then running a nearObject search against that collection with a beacon pointing into a collection they do not control, a caller can recover the protected vector to a high degree of precision. The reporter demonstrated recovery of a normalized four-dimensional vector to within 5e-9 using eight probe objects.

To carry out the attack, a user needs:

  1. The name of the target collection and the UUID of a specific object within it. These are not guessable, but they are often known, for example where an application stores cross-references between collections.
  2. Permission to read collection definitions, which GraphQL requires in order to expose the collection's fields.
  3. Permission to create and read data in some other collection, used to hold the probe vectors.

The user does not need read permission on the target collection. Weaviate correctly returns 403 for a direct read of the protected object while the same account retrieves the same vector through the search path.

This affects deployments that rely on RBAC to separate collections within a shared cluster, for instance where several teams or applications share one Weaviate instance and each has read access only to its own collection. Deployments where every user with query access is already trusted with all collection data are not meaningfully affected.

The fix authorizes the beacon target before its vector is loaded, at the shared vector lookup rather than in the GraphQL resolver, so that every API surface using that lookup is covered by the same check.

The CVSS score for this vulnerability is Medium.

Impacted versions of Weaviate are < v1.39.3. We recommend that impacted users update their Weaviate installations to v1.39.3 or later to fully address the vulnerability. Until you can upgrade, we recommend reviewing which roles hold read_collections across all collections, since a user who cannot see a collection's definition cannot query its fields through GraphQL, and narrowing that permission to the collections each role legitimately needs. Reviewing which roles hold create_data on any collection is also worthwhile, as the attack requires somewhere to place probe vectors.

We have no indication that this vulnerability has been exploited.

Acknowledgements​

This vulnerability was discovered and reported by Civitasmass, who notified us through our Vulnerability Disclosure Program. The report included a complete working reproducer and a precise root cause analysis, which allowed us to confirm and fix the issue quickly. We would like to thank them for reporting it responsibly.

item.title: PathSeer: Adaptive Filtered Vector Search
item.description: Weaviate 1.40 adds PathSeer, a third HNSW filter strategy from a SIGMOD 2026 paper, contributed by the paper's first author. How it works, and how it compares to sweeping and ACORN.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction​

Most vector search use-cases have need for filtered vector search and it can be argued this is the most popular query type. A filtered vector search combines a semantic query such as books about architecture with structured criteria like published_date > 2000 or language = 'en'.

There are many ways to approach this problem with vector indices. One set of approaches are filter aware, you define what filters will be used upfront. Filter aware approaches perform very well on low-cardinality static data, but do not work well in a dynamic environment where filters (and even the schema) change over time. The other set of approaches (like ACORN) can be termed filter (or predicate) agnostic, and generally amount to different ways to explore the ANN neighbour graph.

In late 2024, we were one of the first vector databases to ship ACORN as an HNSW filter strategy, and it became the default in 1.34. ACORN performs particularly well when filters are negatively correlated, however it loses recall on very sparse filters, and above 40% selectivity its two-hop expansion costs more than it saves, so we restricted ACORN based on selectivity.

We felt there were still improvements available and so were pleasantly surprised when Zhiyue Li, Guangyan Zhang and colleagues at Tsinghua University announced their SIGMOD 2026 paper PathSeer: Adaptive Neighbor Handling for Efficient Filtered ANN Search. The paper describes PathSeer, a new predicate-agnostic filtered vector search algorithm in HNSW with large performance improvements over other strategies.

As part of their research, Zhiyue Li added PathSeer to Weaviate. In this blog we will go through the algorithm and showcase performance improvements, and how to use it in Weaviate 1.40.

How to handle a neighbor​

When using graph-based ANN techniques like HNSW, candidates are found using a beam search algorithm which determines the order in which new nodes get explored.

With unfiltered vector search this is relatively easy - just compute the distance calculation between the query vector and candidate vector. However with filtered vector search there are more decisions to make.

One important decision is: do you compute the distance first or check the filter first?

The PathSeer paper names these two options:

  • Distance first (DFN). Compute the distance to every neighbor and push it to the candidate heap. Check the filter when a neighbor is good enough to enter the result set. This is equivalent to Weaviate's sweeping strategy. It ensures the graph never disconnects, but at low selectivity most of the distance computations are wasted on nodes that don't pass the filter.
  • Filter first (DOS). Check the filter on every neighbor and only calculate distances for the ones that pass. This is in essence ACORN. It avoids wasted distance calculations but has potential to disconnect the graph leading to lower recall. One insight from ACORN is to use 2-hop neighbors, i.e. check if a neighbor matches the filter or any of its neighbors. It tends to work well in low-selectivity filters but at high selectivity the two hops multiply the number of filter checks needed.

The paper measured both strategies on six workloads and found the best choice varied by dataset, depending on how selective a filter was and how expensive the filter check was compared to the distance calculation.

In Weaviate we resolve the filter against the inverted index into a roaring bitmap before the vector search starts. This ensures that the filter check is just a bitmap lookup (around 17 ns), regardless of how complex the original filter was. The distance computation will cost roughly 50 - 110 ns dependent on quantization and size of the vector.

Introducing PathSeer​

PathSeer's answer to this is to decide the strategy per node dynamically.

In the paper PathSeer splits each node's neighbor list in two. The sparse zone has the usual pruned HNSW neighbors and is always explored distance first. The expanding zone has extra, unpruned neighbors sorted by distance. The expanding zone is walked filter first until a predefined budget is passed where it switches to distance first. The result is a mixture of filter first and distance first computations with no per query tuning.

In the authors' Faiss implementation this gave 1.2 to 13.5 times the throughput of plain HNSW, and 1.6 to 10.6 times the throughput of ACORN, at 90% recall@10, for selectivities from 100% down to 0.1%.

Zhiyue Li, one of the authors of the PathSeer paper created the original Weaviate PR, however with notable improvements to compatibility:

  • In the new approach, separate neighbor lists are no longer needed and PathSeer is compatible with normal HNSW indices.
  • This allows for filter strategies to be changed on an existing HNSW index - no rebuild required.

In the modified approach there are two phases:

  1. Two-hop burst. While the heap has fewer than ef entries, each popped node also adds its two hop neighbors that match the filter. This operates as the expanding zone, but is taken from the existing graph. It stops once the heap is full, so it does not multiply filter checks for the rest of the search.
  2. Once the heap is full, skip distances between non-matching nodes. When a popped node does not match the filter, its neighbors that also don't match are skipped, with no distance computed. When the popped node does match, all its neighbors get distances as in sweeping, matching or not. The second half is important: non-matching nodes next to matching ones stay in the search as bridges, so it can still cross regions where nothing matches. Skipped nodes are not marked visited, so another path can still reach them later.

Benchmarks​

The below benchmarks used a Weaviate 1.40 build on a GCP c4-standard-16 (16 vCPUs, 60 GB Memory) instance. The Weaviate benchmarker tool was used, in particular with flat search cutoff disabled, so we could test the filtered ANN performance even when normally the filter would be restrictive enough to trigger a brute force search.

Three sources for filtered datasets are used.

  • BEIR Cohere. The sets from the ACORN post: 500k Cohere v3 embeddings mixed from the NQ and MS MARCO corpora, with a filter on the MS MARCO share, plus a 1.1M set of 22 BEIR corpora with a filter on the source corpus.
  • Sphere DPR. 1M 768-dimension embeddings with uniformly random categories.
  • wiki-dpr 10M. 10M Wiki passages from e5-base-v2 embeddings on Hugging Face, with 27 generated filters (random, topical, and conjunction) and exact filtered ground truth for each.

Topical filters​

First we use a filtered dataset using Cohere v3 embeddings from BEIR that we used previously to evaluate ACORN. We combine two datasets (NQ and MSMARCO) and vary the percentage to change the selectivity of the filter.

In this dataset PathSeer matches or beats both sweeping and ACORN at every selectivity range.

Here is a QPS vs recall graph showing 20% selectivity (20% of the dataset matches the filter) and low correlation (the query vector is not part of the filter).

Next, and importantly, here is a graph showing again at 20% selectivity what happens when the query vector is part of the filter region. This is the scenario where previously sweeping would outperform ACORN, however here PathSeer outperforms both.

On the wiki-dpr 10M dataset we see PathSeer clearly outperforms ACORN and also exceeds sweeping on topical filters (built here by clustering the article embeddings, so the matching passages form a region of the graph).

Note that at 0.1% selectivity Weaviate would normally switch to a brute force search over the filter set (the default flatSearchCutoff is 40,000 objects), which is the better choice at that size.

Conjunction filters​

The conjunction filters are the ones closest to a production filter: a semantic attribute combined with a range on something orthogonal, such as a date or a tenant. On wiki-dpr each one is a topical filter AND a range on the object id, which breaks the link between where a passage sits in the embedding space and where it sits in the index. Six of them span 55k to 911k passages.

PathSeer is the fastest strategy at 0.90 recall on all six, by 1.1 to 1.4 times over the better of sweeping and ACORN. ACORN reaches 0.90 on only three of them.

On this 238k-passage conjunction PathSeer is 1.36 times sweeping at 0.90 recall and reaches 0.98 at ef 512, while ACORN tops out at 0.86.

The larger conjunction, 532k passages at 5.3% selectivity, is dense enough for ACORN to reach 0.90 recall, and PathSeer is still ahead of both: 1.3 times sweeping and 1.7 times ACORN at 0.90, with a recall ceiling of 0.98 against ACORN's 0.93.

Random filters​

Random filters are where the filter has zero correlation with the query. They are the easiest test datasets to generate (just randomly assign each vector to a cluster based on the desired selectivity).

Here the filter carries no semantic information, so we can't deliberately move to a region with more vectors passing the filter, which most exposes ACORN. In these examples we see PathSeer degrade to sweeping, with an improvement at very low selectivity.

Negatively correlated filters​

Finally the most difficult case is where the query is strongly negatively correlated with the filter. In this case, the distance calculations point the beam search in the wrong direction (towards better ANN results but fewer filter matches) and this has historically been a major reason for recommending ACORN.

Here we see ACORN still heavily outperforming sweeping, and also outperforming PathSeer, though by a much smaller margin.

One property PathSeer keeps from sweeping is that recall continues to climb with ef. At ef 2048 PathSeer reaches 0.998 recall on this dataset while ACORN plateaus at 0.984, so for very high recall targets on a filter like this PathSeer is the graph strategy that gets there.

To put a number on "correlated", we measured for each dataset what share of a query's unfiltered top-10 neighbors pass the filter, divided by the filter's selectivity. A value of 1 means the filter is independent of the query, above 1 the filter favors the query's neighborhood, and below 1 it excludes it.

Using PathSeer​

PathSeer ships in Weaviate 1.40 as a value of the existing filterStrategy setting on the HNSW index. The default remains acorn.

"vectorIndexConfig": {
  "filterStrategy": "pathseer"
}

The setting is mutable, so an existing collection can be switched without reindexing. The flatSearchCutoff setting still applies before any strategy: filters matching fewer objects than the cutoff are brute-forced as before.

With the Python client, set the strategy when creating a collection:

from weaviate.classes.config import Configure, VectorFilterStrategy

client.collections.create(
    "Article",
    vector_index_config=Configure.VectorIndex.hnsw(
        filter_strategy=VectorFilterStrategy.PATHSEER,
    ),
)

Or switch an existing collection:

from weaviate.classes.config import Reconfigure, VectorFilterStrategy

articles = client.collections.use("Article")
articles.config.update(
    vector_index_config=Reconfigure.VectorIndex.hnsw(
        filter_strategy=VectorFilterStrategy.PATHSEER,
    ),
)

Conclusion​

PathSeer is the fastest filter strategy in Weaviate on almost every workload we tested, and it holds up where ACORN loses recall and where sweeping loses throughput. It needs no reindexing and no new parameters: set filterStrategy to pathseer on an existing collection and it takes effect immediately. Try it on your own filters in Weaviate 1.40 and let us know how it performs.

item.title: Weaviate security release - High severity fix for credential disclosure in the Google modules
item.description: Weaviate v1.39.3 fixes a high-severity credential disclosure issue in the Google modules.
item.content:encoded:
Intro​

Weaviate v1.39.3 includes a fix for a high severity credential disclosure vulnerability in Weaviate's Google-backed modules, where an unvalidated endpoint setting could be used to redirect an outbound request, and the operator's Google credential with it, to an arbitrary host. A CVE has been requested from MITRE and is pending assignment; we will update this post with the CVE ID once it has been issued.

As per our security policy, Weaviate customers running in Weaviate Cloud, and Marketplace customers on AWS, Azure and GCP have been patched seamlessly. Our Weaviate Enterprise Support customers have received early notification under embargo, and our customer-facing teams are working with Weaviate Dedicated customers to organize version upgrades where appropriate.

Credential disclosure via unvalidated apiEndpoint in the Google modules (CVE pending assignment)​

Weaviate's Google-backed modules (text2vec-google, multi2vec-google and generative-google) allow the host used for outbound Vertex AI and Gemini requests to be set through an apiEndpoint configuration value. That value was written directly into the host portion of the request URL without validation, and the operator's configured Google credential was attached to the request as a bearer token regardless of where the request was being sent. A user who can influence apiEndpoint could therefore cause Weaviate to deliver that credential to a host of their choosing.

There were two paths to setting the value:

  1. Through collection configuration. Setting moduleConfig.text2vec-google.apiEndpoint (or the equivalent for the other two modules) when creating or updating a collection. Validation at this layer checked only that a project ID was present; the endpoint string itself was never checked. This path requires schema-write privileges.
  2. Through a GraphQL query parameter. generative-google accepted apiEndpoint as an inline parameter on a generative query, and the per-query value overrode the collection default. This path requires only ordinary read access to a collection already configured to use generative-google, with no schema-write privilege and no change to stored configuration.

The second path is the more serious of the two, and is the main reason for the severity rating.

The credential exposed depends on how the deployment authenticates to Google. Where a static API key is configured, that key is disclosed. Where USE_GOOGLE_AUTH is enabled, the disclosed value is a live OAuth access token scoped to cloud-platform, which is broad enough to reach most Google Cloud APIs available to the underlying service account. This is the documented way to run Vertex AI vectorization using Google Cloud Application Default Credentials, and the usual arrangement for GKE deployments using Workload Identity.

This is a distinct code path from the base URL validation added in earlier releases. That work hardened the endpoint fields of a large number of other model providers, but those fields are named baseURL; the Google modules' field is named apiEndpoint and was not covered. The related dial-time protection is also opt-in via MODULES_VALIDATE_BASE_URL and blocks only loopback, private and link-local addresses, so it does not prevent a credential being sent to an attacker-controlled host on the public internet.

The fix extends endpoint validation to the apiEndpoint field in all three Google modules, at both the configuration-validation layer and the GraphQL query-parameter layer.

The CVSS score for this vulnerability is High (7.1).

Impacted versions of Weaviate are < v1.39.3. We recommend that impacted users update their Weaviate installations to v1.39.3 or later to fully address the vulnerability. Until you can upgrade, the affected modules can be disabled by removing text2vec-google, multi2vec-google and generative-google from the "enabled_modules" flag. Where the modules are required, we recommend restricting schema-write and query access to collections configured to use them, and scoping the service account used for Vertex AI as narrowly as your workload allows rather than relying on a broad cloud-platform scope.

We have no indication that this vulnerability has been exploited.

Acknowledgements​

This vulnerability was discovered and reported by Syed Anas Mohiuddin, an independent security researcher, who notified us through our Vulnerability Disclosure Program. We would like to thank him for the detail and care of the report, and for working with us through validation and remediation.

item.title: 4-bit Rotational Quantization
item.description: 4-bit Rotational Quantization in Weaviate 1.39: the SIMD performance work, a centered tier, scaling analysis and a TurboQuant comparison.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction​

Last year we introduced Rotational Quantization (or RQ) with 8-bit and 1-bit sizes. These quantization techniques allow for fast vector search, while reducing memory usage, and at better recall than comparable alternatives such as scalar and binary quantization.

Weaviate 1.39 extends RQ with 4-bit support, alongside a stack of quantization improvements in general. Rotations, distance kernels, encoding and the memory path have all been improved with net effect: 8-bit RQ is now significantly faster in 1.39 and 4-bit RQ provides similar recall with a 45% heap reduction.

This post documents the story of that work, and along the way answers two questions people often ask: How does RQ hold up as datasets scale? And how does RQ compare to TurboQuant?

Improvements​

Rotational quantization is based on Extended-RaBitQ with a structured fast rotation and simplified per-vector interval fitting to speed up encoding. Fast encoding performance (converting the original vector into its quantized representation) is an important part of a good quantization algorithm as it can have significant impacts on import performance.

The first step in these approaches is to multiply the original vector by a random rotation matrix. It may seem counter-intuitive but a random rotation matrix gives better properties to the vector in particular distributing the dimension values over the entire length of the quantization interval.

To speed up the random rotation we use Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transforms (FWHT) to rotate the original vector. In 1.39, we added SIMD support for FWHT which led to the below improvements while being bit-identical to the Go reference:

Distance kernels​

The distance kernels were adapted to 4-bits via use of SIMD nibble (half byte) functions. We also switched to UDOT (arm64) and VPDPBUSD (amd64) byte dot functions where possible, which also improved 8-bit quantization. Note the distance functions of 8-bit and 4-bit are similar but there is a big impact on memory bandwidth as explained in the following section.

Single query→code distance computation (cosine), 1.38 vs 1.39:

RQ8Intel Xeon 8581C (amd64/AVX2)76834.3 ns16.6 ns2.1×

RQ8Apple M1 (arm64/NEON)102431.1 ns20.0 ns1.6×
RQ4 (uncentered)Apple M1 (arm64/NEON)768—17.8 nsnew in 1.39
RQ4 (uncentered)Apple M1 (arm64/NEON)1024—21.0 nsnew in 1.39
RQ4 (centered)Apple M1 (arm64/NEON)768—24.5 nsnew in 1.39
RQ4 (centered)Apple M1 (arm64/NEON)1024—27.0 nsnew in 1.39

Prefetching and memory access​

To achieve sub 30ns distance kernels we also need the vectors to be cached effectively by the CPU cache. As graph ANN indices (like HNSW) have scattered DRAM access, memory bandwidth is often the primary bottleneck in performance - not the distance calculation itself.

To improve this in 1.39, we added efficient prefetching for both AMD64 and ARM64 architectures (and fixed a prefetching bug in AMD64 that was many years old). Prefetching helps by hinting to the processor what vectors will be used next. As HNSW expands to compute distances of neighbours we now prefetch or hint ahead of a batch of vector distance computations.

On a 1M-vector index (d=1536, ~800 MB of compressed codes, far beyond CPU cache), an A/B with only the prefetch hints removed shows they contribute 7–11% query throughput (growing with ef) and 12% faster imports.

Centering and outliers​

With the pipeline at hardware speed, we went looking for recall headroom at 4-bits. One open item was centering which we knew can add recall to many embedding datasets. Centering exploits the fact many embeddings have a non-zero mean vector. We compute this mean μ on a subset of the vectors and then encode x − μ against a single mean fitted at compression time, centering the query with the same mean, and add the cross-term back.

On many datasets centering showed significant recall improvements with recall@10 increasing by +0.1 to +6.1pp across several datasets, as embeddings tend to be anisotropic, particularly late-interaction models. However some embedding models are regularized to remove this mean so we make the feature opt-in via a flag centering=true.

Additionally, when quantizing a vector the most extreme rotated coordinates add quantization noise to every dimension in that vector. By storing the largest two magnitude coordinates exactly, we managed to add +0.2 to +1.7pp recall on top of centering, and by careful packing of metadata bytes, we found we could store this in the standard 16 byte metadata header we already have.

Results​

Recall​

The below table shows the recall@10 achievable by each quantization method. This table shows brute force recall excluding the ANN index to isolate the effect on quantization itself.

DatasetRQ4 recall@10 / rescored@20RQ4c recall@10 / rescored@20RQ8 recall@10 / rescored@20
dbpedia-ada002-1536-1M (cosine)93.5 / 100.096.8 / 100.099.0 / 100.0
sphere-dpr-768-1M (dot)90.9 / 99.496.3 / 100.098.2 / 100.0
sift-128-1M (l2)81.4 / 97.287.5 / 99.396.7 / 99.9
glove-100-1.2M (cosine)87.0 / 99.289.9 / 99.898.5 / 100.0
dbpedia-cohere-v2-4096-500k (dot)98.1 / 100.098.5 / 100.099.9 / 100.0
msmarco-arctic-embed-m-768-1M (cosine)94.7 / 100.095.8 / 100.099.3 / 100.0
